title: Bearing with others (I.16)
hookLine: bear with others' faults, since you have your own
tomorrow: what's sweet about a room where nothing happens?

cards: Why put up with someone's worst habit? The Imitation gives an odd answer for a book about becoming holy.
Whatever you can't fix in yourself or in someone else, it says, bear it patiently until God arranges things otherwise. Then it adds: maybe it's better that way. Better?
This is a book that just spent pages on rooting out faults. Now it says some should be left standing, at least for a while. Why would a manual for improvement tell anyone to stop fixing a person?

teach.b: Chapter sixteen of book one gives two reasons, and the second is the twist. First, patience. Without patience being tested, the book says, our good deeds don't weigh much.
The friend who's always late is, among other things, a trainer. Annoying, and useful. Second, the mirror.

Be patient with other people's faults, it says, because you have plenty that others have to put up with. If you can't make yourself the way you want to be, how can you expect someone else to be exactly to your liking?
Then it catches us in the act. We want others perfect, and don't fix our own faults. We want them strictly corrected, and won't be corrected ourselves.
So the puzzle solves itself: the habit you can't fix in someone else sits right next to one of yours that they can't fix either. And then the surprise.
God set things up this way on purpose, the chapter says, so we'd learn to carry each other's loads, and it quotes Paul.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ."
Then the reason, in four short phrases: no one is without fault, no one without a burden, no one is enough for themselves, no one wise enough alone.
Not a team of perfect people. A team of people carrying each other.

how: Catholics count bearing wrongs patiently among the spiritual works of mercy, and religious communities in particular speak of mutual forbearance as part of daily life together.

o: patience with others' faults, since you have yours
putting up with people until you can leave
keeping quiet about any wrong someone does

games.q: the chapter on bearing — tap the pairs.

s: the Imitation says to fix other people's faults first
it says we want others perfect and don't amend our own.
the chapter quotes Paul: bear ye one another's burdens
it quotes Galatians, and says God arranged things so we'd learn to carry each other's loads.
a holy community is one where nobody has faults
the chapter says no one is without fault, and no one without a burden.

games.q: your roommate leaves dishes in the sink every night. you've asked twice. by chapter sixteen, what comes next?
o: bear it for now, and look at what they're putting up with in you.
post a passive-aggressive note until it stops.
keep a list so you can prove the pattern later.
games.why: the chapter says bear patiently what you can't fix, because you have faults that others bear too. bearing runs both ways.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one habit of someone else that wears on you. Underneath it, write one of your own that someone puts up with. Look at the two lines together for the rest of the sit, No need to fix either one yet.
If you pray, ask for patience with both.

wordCard.voice: Bearing with others. The Imitation's counsel: be patient with other people's faults, since they're bearing with yours.

orig.note: Latin: bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2), the line the Imitation quotes in its chapter on bearing with others.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: you have yours, and somebody out there is carrying them with you. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ.
